16	quirks:
17	  - "⛔⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR: THE FIRST REQUEST TO POST /api/install, AND NOTHING CLOSES THAT WINDOW EXCEPT DOING IT YOURSELF. Verified in server/src/core/server/app/handlers/api/install.ts:186-254: one unauthenticated POST creates the tenant, creates the site, and creates the first user WITH ROLE ADMIN. The only guard is whether a tenant already exists. There is no setup token, no environment variable and no config flag that gates the first install: the MANAGEMENT_SIGNING_SECRET path at :169-183 sits INSIDE the `if (alreadyInstalled)` branch, so it only permits ADDITIONAL tenants later and adds nothing to the first one. Coral is one-shot, exactly like Dify, and Dify shipped in this library without this quirk and sat claimable on a public hostname until a human noticed. SO: RUN THE INSTALL YOURSELF, AS PART OF THE DEPLOY, BEFORE YOU HAND OVER THE URL. The script in the body of this file does it and then proves the window is shut. Never report this deployment as ready while GET /api/install still answers 204."
18	  - "⛔ INSTALL THROUGH THE PUBLIC HOSTNAME, NOT THROUGH localhost OR THE VM's IP. install.ts:214-226 records the tenant's domain as `req.hostname`, taken from the request that performed the install, and server/src/core/server/app/router/api/index.ts:58-61 states that every request past the tenant middleware can only proceed if there is a valid Tenant FOR THAT HOSTNAME. Install over an SSH tunnel to localhost and you get a tenant whose domain is `localhost`, after which the public URL has no tenant, the install route says it is already installed, and the only way out is editing MongoDB or starting over. Generate the dname up front in full coral-<8 lowercase alphanumeric>.redu.cloud form and run the install against https://that-name."
19	  - "⛔⛔ SIGNING_SECRET, AND THE DEFAULT IS A JOKE THAT UPSTREAM DEFENDS AGAINST. config.ts:211-212 defaults it to the literal string \"keyboard cat\". docs/docs/environment-variables.md:29-33 says Coral throws a runtime error rather than start when NODE_ENV=production and the secret is still that default, and the image sets NODE_ENV=production (Dockerfile:74), so this is one of the rare traps in this library that fails LOUDLY: the container will not boot. Generate it once with `openssl rand -base64 45`, keep it with the deployment, and reuse the identical value on every redeploy. Changing it signs every JSON Web Token with a new key, which logs out every moderator and every reader at once and invalidates any outstanding password-reset, email-confirmation and invite link. Nothing is decrypted with it, so nothing is permanently lost; everyone simply has to sign in again."
20	  - "⛔⛔ THERE IS NO MANAGED MONGODB ON REDU, SO YOUR DATA LIVES ON THE APP VM AND SHARES ITS LIFETIME. Say this to the user BEFORE they approve the plan, because it is the one way this entry differs from every other one in the library. Coral keeps every comment, every reader account, every moderation decision and the tenant configuration itself in MongoDB, and here MongoDB is a container on the app VM writing to a Docker volume on that VM's disk. Consequences, plainly: delete_deployment destroys the comments along with the app, because there is no managed database standing behind it; anything that replaces the VM rather than restarting the container takes the data with it; and there is no point-in-time restore, no automatic backup and no second copy anywhere unless you make one. SO MAKE ONE, and put it in the handover: `sudo docker exec <mongo-container> mongodump --archive --db=coral | gzip > coral-$(date +%F).archive.gz` run from the VM, copied off the VM, on a schedule the user chooses. Take one before every redeploy and before every image bump. The 80 GB disk on m1.large exists partly for this reason."
21	  - "⚠️ MONGODB 5.0 AND LATER REQUIRE THE AVX INSTRUCTION SET, AND NOBODY HAS RUN MONGODB ON REDU YET, SO CHECK IT FIRST RATHER THAN DEBUGGING IT LATER. If the guest CPU model presented to the VM masks AVX, the mongo container exits immediately and the log says \"Illegal instruction\", which does not read like a CPU feature problem at all and can cost an hour. This is an upstream MongoDB requirement, not a redu claim, and it is UNVERIFIED on this platform. Check it in the first minute, both halves: on the VM run `grep -c avx /proc/cpuinfo` and expect a number greater than 0 (the positive half, which also proves your command ran), THEN `sudo docker logs <mongo-container>` and confirm it reports waiting for connections. If AVX is missing, stop and say so rather than working around it; mongo:4.4 is the last version without the requirement and Coral asks for ^8.0.3."
22	  - "⛔ DELETE THE PUBLISHED DATABASE PORTS FROM UPSTREAM'S COMPOSE. Their root docker-compose.yml publishes 27017:27017 and 6379:6379 on the host, which is a local-development convenience: it contains no Coral service at all, only mongo and redis. This MongoDB has no authentication configured and this Redis has no password, which is fine on a private compose network and is not fine on any interface you do not control. In the compose in this file the two datastores have NO ports section and are reached by service name over the compose network; only Coral's 5000 is published, and only that one is proxied onto the public hostname."
23	  - "⛔ UPSTREAM'S OWN INSTALLATION PAGE CONTRADICTS ITSELF, AND FOLLOWING ITS COPY-PASTE BLOCK INSTALLS SOMETHING TWO MAJOR VERSIONS OLD. docs/docs/installation.md states the requirements as MongoDB ^8.0.3 and Redis ^3.2, and then, a few lines below, hands you a compose that pins mongo:4.2, redis:3.2 and coralproject/talk:7 while the current release is 9.11.8. Trust the requirements line and the repository's own root compose (mongo:8.0.3, redis:7.2.5), not the snippet. Pin coralproject/talk:9.11.8: the registry tag has NO leading v, unlike the GitHub release which is v9.11.8, and the rolling `9` and `9.11` tags beside it must not go into a recipe."
24	  - "PORT 5000, FROM THE IMAGE, NOT FROM THE DOCUMENTED DEFAULT. config.ts:147-148 defaults PORT to 3000, and Dockerfile:74-76 overrides it to 5000 and exposes 5000. Every tutorial that says 3000 is describing a from-source run. Publish 5000 and pass 5000 to deploy_compose."
25	  - "SET TRUST_PROXY AND LEAVE FORCE_SSL ALONE. redu terminates TLS in front of the container and forwards plain HTTP, so without TRUST_PROXY Coral believes the request arrived over http and writes http:// URLs into the admin and into emails. config.ts:132-137 leaves it empty and app/index.ts:204-212 feeds it to Express's trust proxy setting, so TRUST_PROXY=1 (trust the first hop) is the value you want. Do NOT reach for FORCE_SSL to fix a URL problem: upstream's own docs warn it causes redirect loops when the proxy is not trusted, and it also emits a 60-day HSTS header, which is a commitment you cannot take back for two months. The public hostname is already HTTPS-only."
26	  - "⛔ MONGODB_URI AND REDIS_URI MUST BOTH BE SET, AND REDU INJECTS NEITHER. config.ts:178-199 defaults them to 127.0.0.1, which inside the app container is the app container itself, so an unset value is a connection refused at boot rather than a silent fallback. There is no SQLite trap here and no managed database to wire: point them at the compose service names, mongodb://mongo:[REDACTED:conn-password]/coral and redis://redis:[REDACTED:conn-password] Because there is no managed Postgres in this deployment, redu's one-database-per-managed-server rule and db_superuser do not apply at all, and deploy_compose is called WITHOUT a database argument."
27	  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH, AND MOST OF IT IS THE PRODUCT WORKING. Coral is a public commenting system: the comment stream, the embed script, story pages and the comment counts are all meant to be world-readable, and /api/graphql serves the stream's queries to signed-out readers. Beyond that: GET /api/health returns a static 200 (handlers/api/health.ts is three lines and touches nothing), GET /api/version returns the version, and GET /api/install answers 204 or 400. /graphiql is OFF unless ENABLE_GRAPHIQL is set, and the Prometheus endpoint lives on its own port (METRICS_PORT, default 9000) which this compose does not publish, which matters because METRICS_USERNAME and METRICS_PASSWORD are both empty by default and an empty pair means NO authentication on it. Moderation, admin and every account action require a token."
28	  - "REGISTRATION IS OPEN AFTER THE INSTALL, BY DESIGN, AND EMAIL IS OFF, WHICH IS THE PART TO SAY OUT LOUD. models/tenant/tenant.ts:192-202 gives a fresh tenant local auth ENABLED with allowRegistration TRUE on both the stream and the admin target, and :239-242 leaves email DISABLED. So any reader can create an account and comment the moment you finish the install, which is what a commenting platform is for, but with no mailer configured there is no address confirmation, no password reset and no notification mail: accounts are created against unverified addresses. Two consequences to hand over. First, if the admin password is lost there is NO recovery path until SMTP is configured in Settings, so keep it. Second, decide with the user whether the stream should be pre-moderated on day one, and configure SMTP in the admin before inviting anyone."
29	  - "allowedOrigins IS WHERE THE STREAM IS EMBEDDED, NOT WHERE CORAL LIVES, AND THAT IS THE ONE FIELD OF THE INSTALL THAT NEEDS THE USER'S ANSWER. app/middleware/csp.ts:139-165 turns a site's allowedOrigins into the frame-ancestors CSP for the comment stream, so it must list the ORIGINS OF THE WEBSITE the comments appear on, for example https://www.theirsite.com. Putting only the redu hostname in there produces a Coral that installs cleanly, serves its admin perfectly, and refuses to render inside their actual page. Ask which domains before you install; more can be added in the admin afterwards."
30	  - "⚠️ LIVE COMMENT UPDATES USE A WEBSOCKET AND NOBODY HAS CONFIRMED REDU'S PROXY UPGRADES IT. Coral's stream subscribes over /api/graphql/live. If the upgrade does not pass through, the failure is quiet: comments still post and still appear on reload, they simply do not stream in. config.ts:267-274 provides the honest fallback, DISABLE_LIVE_UPDATES=true, which turns the feature off across the whole installation and CANNOT be turned back on from the interface, so do not set it pre-emptively. ON THE FIRST REAL DEPLOY, post a comment from a second browser and watch whether it appears without a reload, then write the answer into this file by hand."
31	  - "USERNAME AND PASSWORD RULES FOR THE ADMIN YOU CREATE, BOTH ENFORCED SERVER-SIDE AND BOTH EASY TO TRIP. common/lib/helpers/validate.ts:3-5: the username must match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_.]+$ and be 3 to 30 characters, which means NO HYPHEN: a generated name like coral-admin is rejected outright, so use coral_admin or coraladmin. validate.ts:9: the password minimum is 8 characters. Generate it locally and alphanumeric only, both because this library's rule says so and because the install body is JSON, where an unescaped quote or backslash would make the request invalid rather than merely wrong."
32	  - "/api/health IS A STATIC 200 AND MUST NOT BE USED AS A READINESS CHECK. handlers/api/health.ts is `res.status(200).send(\"OK\")` and nothing else: it reaches neither MongoDB nor Redis, so it goes green while the databases are unreachable and the app is useless. The endpoint that actually proves the stack is GET /api/install, which performs a tenant lookup in MongoDB and passes through a Redis-backed rate limiter, and whose answer also tells you the one thing you care about: 204 means UNCLAIMED, 400 means installed. Note the polarity, because it is the reverse of the usual: on this route the 400 is the good news."
33	  - "NO migrate_command NEEDED. server/src/core/server/index.ts:371-380 runs pending migrations at startup whenever a tenant is already installed, and install.ts:206-211 runs them inside the install call itself for a fresh database. Upgrading Coral is therefore: back up MongoDB, bump the pinned tag, redeploy, and let it migrate on boot. 41	# Self-host Coral on redu
42	
43	Comments on your own site, on your own server: the commenting platform built by Vox Media and used
44	by The Washington Post and the Financial Times, on one VM with its own MongoDB and Redis beside it
45	and a public HTTPS URL. Around GBP 35 a month.
46	
47	## What this deploys
48	
49	- **Coral** from the official image, pinned to `9.11.8`, on one m1.large VM, port 5000.
50	- **MongoDB** and **Redis** in the same compose, on volumes on that VM.
51	- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS, which is where the comment stream is served from
52	  and where you embed it into your own pages.
53	
54	About GBP 0.049/hour. **Above the no-card trial ceiling**, so this one needs a card.
55	
56	## Read this before you approve the plan
57	
58	**The database lives on the app VM.** redu has no managed MongoDB, so unlike every other entry in
59	this library there is no managed database standing behind this deployment. Every comment, every
60	reader account and every moderation decision sits on the app VM's disk and shares that VM's
61	lifetime.
62	
63	That is workable and it is what upstream's own Docker install does. It just means two things are
64	on you rather than on the platform:
65	
66	- **Take backups.** `mongodump`, copied off the VM, on a schedule you choose, and one before
67	  every redeploy.
68	- **Deleting the deployment deletes the comments.** There is nothing left behind to restore from.
69	
70	## Deploy
71	
72	Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
73	directory containing this file:
74	
75	    Read redu.md and deploy Coral on redu.
76	
77	The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.
78	
79	## The one that would actually break it
80	
81	**Coral has no accounts until somebody runs the installer, and the installer is one unauthenticated
82	POST that makes the caller an administrator.** No token, no environment variable, no setting closes
83	that window. From the moment the hostname answers until somebody claims it, the instance belongs to
84	whoever gets there first.
85	
86	So the install is part of the deploy, not a thing you do afterwards over coffee. The script below
87	does it and then proves the window is shut.
88	
89	Two smaller ones that follow from it:
90	
91	- **Install through the public hostname.** Coral records the tenant's domain from the Host header
92	  of the install request, and looks the tenant up by hostname on every request afterwards. Install
93	  via localhost and the public URL has no tenant at all.
94	- **`allowedOrigins` is your website, not Coral's address.** It becomes the `frame-ancestors`
95	  policy for the stream, so it decides where the comments are allowed to be embedded.
96	
97	## The compose
98	
99	Three services, one published port. Upstream ships no production compose, so this is written from
100	the Dockerfile and the configuration source.
101	
102	```yaml
103	services:
104	  talk:
105	    image: coralproject/talk:9.11.8
106	    restart: unless-stopped
107	    depends_on:
108	      - mongo
109	      - redis
110	    ports:
111	      - "5000:5000"
112	    environment:
113	      NODE_ENV: "production"
114	      PORT: "5000"
115	      MONGODB_URI: "mongodb://mongo:[REDACTED:conn-password]/coral"
116	      REDIS_URI: "redis://redis:[REDACTED:conn-password]"
117	      SIGNING_SECRET: "[REDACTED:value]}"
118	      TRUST_PROXY: "1"
119	      LOGGING_LEVEL: "info"
120	  mongo:
121	    image: mongo:8.0.3
122	    restart: unless-stopped
123	    volumes:
124	      - coral-mongo:/data/db
125	  redis:
126	    image: redis:7.2.5
127	    restart: unless-stopped
128	    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes"]
129	    volumes:
130	      - coral-redis:/data
131	volumes:
132	  coral-mongo:
133	  coral-redis:
134	```
135	
136	`CORAL_SIGNING_SECRET` goes in a `.env` beside it, generated locally with
137	`openssl rand -base64 45`. Note that **neither datastore publishes a port**: they are reached by
138	service name on the compose network. Upstream's root compose publishes both, which is a
139	development convenience and not something to copy onto a server.
140	
141	## Claiming the instance
142	
143	Run this the moment the deploy reports ready, before you hand the URL to anyone.
144	
145	It **proves it is talking to Coral before it asserts anything** (a 502 from the proxy while the
146	container starts is not a pass), it refuses to run if somebody has already installed, and it
147	finishes by actually signing in with the account it created rather than trusting a status code.
148	Exits `2` rather than passing when it cannot tell.
149	
150	```bash
151	#!/usr/bin/env bash
152	# Claim a fresh Coral before anyone else can, then prove the window is shut.
153	#   CORAL_ADMIN_EMAIL=you@example.com CORAL_ADMIN_USERNAME=coral_admin \
154	#   CORAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD=[REDACTED:value] CORAL_ORG_NAME="Your Org" CORAL_ORG_URL=https://www.example.com \
155	#   CORAL_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=https://www.example.com \
156	#     ./claim-coral.sh coral-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
157	# Exit 0 = claimed, 1 = NOT safe / already taken, 2 = inconclusive (may still be starting; re-run).
158	set -eu
159	HOST="${1:?usage: claim-coral.sh <host>}"
160	: "${CORAL_ADMIN_EMAIL:?admin email}"
161	: "${CORAL_ADMIN_USERNAME:?admin username, 3-30 chars of a-z A-Z 0-9 _ . and NO hyphen}"
162	: "${CORAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD:«REDACTED:assigned:953a8a9a» password, at least 8 characters}"
163	: "${CORAL_ORG_NAME:?organisation name}"
164	: "${CORAL_ORG_URL:?organisation url, e.g. https://www.example.com}"
165	: "${CORAL_ALLOWED_ORIGINS:?the site origin the comments get embedded on}"
166	
167	case "$CORAL_ADMIN_USERNAME" in
168	  *[!A-Za-z0-9_.]*) echo "FAIL: username may only contain a-z A-Z 0-9 _ . (no hyphen)." >&2; exit 1 ;;
169	esac
170	case "$CORAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD" in
171	  *[!A-Za-z0-9]*) echo "FAIL: generate the password alphanumeric only; this goes into JSON." >&2; exit 1 ;;
172	esac
173	for v in "$CORAL_ORG_NAME" "$CORAL_ORG_URL" "$CORAL_ALLOWED_ORIGINS" "$CORAL_ADMIN_EMAIL"; do
174	  case "$v" in
175	    *'"'*|*'\'*) echo "FAIL: a quote or backslash in "$v" would corrupt the JSON body." >&2; exit 1 ;;
176	  esac
177	done
178	[ "${#CORAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD}" -ge 8 ] || { echo "FAIL: password must be at least 8 characters." >&2; exit 1; }
179	
180	TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
181	
182	# 1. GATE: is this actually Coral, and is it up? Everything below is vacuous otherwise.
183	code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/ver" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/version")
184	if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
185	  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/version answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
186	  if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
187	    echo "  502 is redu's proxy while the container starts. Re-run; NOT a pass." >&2
188	  fi
189	  exit 2
190	fi
191	grep -q '"version"' "$TMP/ver" || {
192	  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200, but the body is not Coral's version document." >&2
193	  echo "  Something else is answering on this hostname. Do not read this as safe." >&2
194	  exit 2
195	}
196	
197	# 2. Is the instance still unclaimed? 204 = nobody has installed. 400 = someone has.
198	#    This route also touches MongoDB and Redis, which /api/health does not.
199	pre=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/install")
200	case "$pre" in
201	  204) ;;
202	  400) echo "FAIL: this Coral is ALREADY INSTALLED and it was not you." >&2
203	       echo "  Someone else owns the admin account. Do not leave it running: tear it down" >&2
204	       echo "  and redeploy, then claim it within the same step." >&2
205	       exit 1 ;;
206	  *)   echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/install answered HTTP $pre, expected 204 or 400." >&2; exit 2 ;;
207	esac
208	
209	# 3. Claim it. The body goes to curl from a FILE, never in argv, because an argument is
210	#    visible in ps to every user on the box.
211	cat > "$TMP/body.json" <<JSON
212	{
213	  "tenant": {
214	    "organization": {
215	      "name": "$CORAL_ORG_NAME",
216	      "url": "$CORAL_ORG_URL",
217	      "contactEmail": "$CORAL_ADMIN_EMAIL"
218	    },
219	    "locale": "en-US"
220	  },
221	  "site": {
222	    "name": "$CORAL_ORG_NAME",
223	    "allowedOrigins": ["$CORAL_ALLOWED_ORIGINS"]
224	  },
225	  "user": {
226	    "username": "$CORAL_ADMIN_USERNAME",
227	    "password": "[REDACTED:value]",
228	    "email": "$CORAL_ADMIN_EMAIL"
229	  }
230	}
231	JSON
232	
233	inst=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/inst" -w '%{http_code}' \
234	  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
235	  --data-binary @"$TMP/body.json" "https://$HOST/api/install")
236	if [ "$inst" != "204" ]; then
237	  echo "FAIL: POST /api/install answered HTTP $inst, not 204." >&2
238	  echo "  Response: $(cat "$TMP/inst")" >&2
239	  echo "  Common causes: a hyphen in the username, a password under 8 characters," >&2
240	  echo "  a non-URL organisation url, or the per-IP limit of 1 install per 10 seconds." >&2
241	  exit 1
242	fi
243	
244	# 4. NEGATIVE half: the window must now be shut.
245	post=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/install")
246	[ "$post" = "400" ] || {
247	  echo "FAIL: after installing, /api/install still answers HTTP $post." >&2
248	  echo "  The instance may still be claimable. Do not hand out this URL." >&2
249	  exit 1
250	}
251	
252	# 5. POSITIVE half, and it is what makes step 4 mean anything: YOUR account signs in.
253	printf '{"email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CORAL_ADMIN_EMAIL" "$CORAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD" > "$TMP/login.json"
254	login=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/tok" -w '%{http_code}' \
255	  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
256	  --data-binary @"$TMP/login.json" "https://$HOST/api/auth/local")
257	[ "$login" = "200" ] || { echo "FAIL: the admin account does not sign in (HTTP $login)." >&2; exit 1; }
258	grep -q '"token"' "$TMP/tok" || { echo "FAIL: sign-in returned no token." >&2; exit 1; }
259	
260	echo "OK: Coral is installed, the install route now refuses, and your admin account signs in."
261	echo "    Next, in the admin at https://$HOST/admin: configure SMTP (email is OFF by default,"
262	echo "    so there is no password reset until you do), and decide your moderation defaults."
263	```
264	
265	## Deploy log
266	
267	- Not yet deployed. The flavor and the hourly rate above are reasoning from the Dockerfile and
268	  `server/src/core/server/config.ts`, not measurement. The first real run should record the idle
269	  memory of all three containers (upstream publishes no figure), and settle the two open questions
270	  in this file: whether the guest CPU exposes AVX, which MongoDB requires, and whether the live
271	  comments websocket upgrades through redu's proxy. Write all three back here by hand; the
272	  `get_deployment` merge will not add them for you.

---

repo: https://github.com/coralproject/talk
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: coralproject/talk:9.11.8 (plus mongo:8.0.3 and redis:7.2.5 on the same VM)
  port: 5000
  vm: m1.large

bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: coral
quirks:
  - "⛔⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR: THE FIRST REQUEST TO POST /api/install, AND NOTHING CLOSES THAT WINDOW EXCEPT DOING IT YOURSELF. Verified in server/src/core/server/app/handlers/api/install.ts:186-254: one unauthenticated POST creates the tenant, creates the site, and creates the first user WITH ROLE ADMIN. The only guard is whether a tenant already exists. There is no setup token, no environment variable and no config flag that gates the first install: the MANAGEMENT_SIGNING_SECRET path at :169-183 sits INSIDE the `if (alreadyInstalled)` branch, so it only permits ADDITIONAL tenants later and adds nothing to the first one. Coral is one-shot, exactly like Dify, and Dify shipped in this library without this quirk and sat claimable on a public hostname until a human noticed. SO: RUN THE INSTALL YOURSELF, AS PART OF THE DEPLOY, BEFORE YOU HAND OVER THE URL. The script in the body of this file does it and then proves the window is shut. Never report this deployment as ready while GET /api/install still answers 204."
  - "⛔ INSTALL THROUGH THE PUBLIC HOSTNAME, NOT THROUGH localhost OR THE VM's IP. install.ts:214-226 records the tenant's domain as `req.hostname`, taken from the request that performed the install, and server/src/core/server/app/router/api/index.ts:58-61 states that every request past the tenant middleware can only proceed if there is a valid Tenant FOR THAT HOSTNAME. Install over an SSH tunnel to localhost and you get a tenant whose domain is `localhost`, after which the public URL has no tenant, the install route says it is already installed, and the only way out is editing MongoDB or starting over. Generate the dname up front in full coral-<8 lowercase alphanumeric>.redu.cloud form and run the install against https://that-name."
  - "⛔⛔ SIGNING_SECRET, AND THE DEFAULT IS A JOKE THAT UPSTREAM DEFENDS AGAINST. config.ts:211-212 defaults it to the literal string \"keyboard cat\". docs/docs/environment-variables.md:29-33 says Coral throws a runtime error rather than start when NODE_ENV=production and the secret is still that default, and the image sets NODE_ENV=production (Dockerfile:74), so this is one of the rare traps in this library that fails LOUDLY: the container will not boot. Generate it once with `openssl rand -base64 45`, keep it with the deployment, and reuse the identical value on every redeploy. Changing it signs every JSON Web Token with a new key, which logs out every moderator and every reader at once and invalidates any outstanding password-reset, email-confirmation and invite link. Nothing is decrypted with it, so nothing is permanently lost; everyone simply has to sign in again."
  - "⛔⛔ THERE IS NO MANAGED MONGODB ON REDU, SO YOUR DATA LIVES ON THE APP VM AND SHARES ITS LIFETIME. Say this to the user BEFORE they approve the plan, because it is the one way this entry differs from every other one in the library. Coral keeps every comment, every reader account, every moderation decision and the tenant configuration itself in MongoDB, and here MongoDB is a container on the app VM writing to a Docker volume on that VM's disk. Consequences, plainly: delete_deployment destroys the comments along with the app, because there is no managed database standing behind it; anything that replaces the VM rather than restarting the container takes the data with it; and there is no point-in-time restore, no automatic backup and no second copy anywhere unless you make one. SO MAKE ONE, and put it in the handover: `sudo docker exec <mongo-container> mongodump --archive --db=coral | gzip > coral-$(date +%F).archive.gz` run from the VM, copied off the VM, on a schedule the user chooses. Take one before every redeploy and before every image bump. The 80 GB disk on m1.large exists partly for this reason."
  - "⚠️ MONGODB 5.0 AND LATER REQUIRE THE AVX INSTRUCTION SET, AND NOBODY HAS RUN MONGODB ON REDU YET, SO CHECK IT FIRST RATHER THAN DEBUGGING IT LATER. If the guest CPU model presented to the VM masks AVX, the mongo container exits immediately and the log says \"Illegal instruction\", which does not read like a CPU feature problem at all and can cost an hour. This is an upstream MongoDB requirement, not a redu claim, and it is UNVERIFIED on this platform. Check it in the first minute, both halves: on the VM run `grep -c avx /proc/cpuinfo` and expect a number greater than 0 (the positive half, which also proves your command ran), THEN `sudo docker logs <mongo-container>` and confirm it reports waiting for connections. If AVX is missing, stop and say so rather than working around it; mongo:4.4 is the last version without the requirement and Coral asks for ^8.0.3."
  - "⛔ DELETE THE PUBLISHED DATABASE PORTS FROM UPSTREAM'S COMPOSE. Their root docker-compose.yml publishes 27017:27017 and 6379:6379 on the host, which is a local-development convenience: it contains no Coral service at all, only mongo and redis. This MongoDB has no authentication configured and this Redis has no password, which is fine on a private compose network and is not fine on any interface you do not control. In the compose in this file the two datastores have NO ports section and are reached by service name over the compose network; only Coral's 5000 is published, and only that one is proxied onto the public hostname."
  - "⛔ UPSTREAM'S OWN INSTALLATION PAGE CONTRADICTS ITSELF, AND FOLLOWING ITS COPY-PASTE BLOCK INSTALLS SOMETHING TWO MAJOR VERSIONS OLD. docs/docs/installation.md states the requirements as MongoDB ^8.0.3 and Redis ^3.2, and then, a few lines below, hands you a compose that pins mongo:4.2, redis:3.2 and coralproject/talk:7 while the current release is 9.11.8. Trust the requirements line and the repository's own root compose (mongo:8.0.3, redis:7.2.5), not the snippet. Pin coralproject/talk:9.11.8: the registry tag has NO leading v, unlike the GitHub release which is v9.11.8, and the rolling `9` and `9.11` tags beside it must not go into a recipe."
  - "PORT 5000, FROM THE IMAGE, NOT FROM THE DOCUMENTED DEFAULT. config.ts:147-148 defaults PORT to 3000, and Dockerfile:74-76 overrides it to 5000 and exposes 5000. Every tutorial that says 3000 is describing a from-source run. Publish 5000 and pass 5000 to deploy_compose."
  - "SET TRUST_PROXY AND LEAVE FORCE_SSL ALONE. redu terminates TLS in front of the container and forwards plain HTTP, so without TRUST_PROXY Coral believes the request arrived over http and writes http:// URLs into the admin and into emails. config.ts:132-137 leaves it empty and app/index.ts:204-212 feeds it to Express's trust proxy setting, so TRUST_PROXY=1 (trust the first hop) is the value you want. Do NOT reach for FORCE_SSL to fix a URL problem: upstream's own docs warn it causes redirect loops when the proxy is not trusted, and it also emits a 60-day HSTS header, which is a commitment you cannot take back for two months. The public hostname is already HTTPS-only."
  - "⛔ MONGODB_URI AND REDIS_URI MUST BOTH BE SET, AND REDU INJECTS NEITHER. config.ts:178-199 defaults them to 127.0.0.1, which inside the app container is the app container itself, so an unset value is a connection refused at boot rather than a silent fallback. There is no SQLite trap here and no managed database to wire: point them at the compose service names, mongodb://mongo:[REDACTED:conn-password]/coral and redis://redis:[REDACTED:conn-password] Because there is no managed Postgres in this deployment, redu's one-database-per-managed-server rule and db_superuser do not apply at all, and deploy_compose is called WITHOUT a database argument."
  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH, AND MOST OF IT IS THE PRODUCT WORKING. Coral is a public commenting system: the comment stream, the embed script, story pages and the comment counts are all meant to be world-readable, and /api/graphql serves the stream's queries to signed-out readers. Beyond that: GET /api/health returns a static 200 (handlers/api/health.ts is three lines and touches nothing), GET /api/version returns the version, and GET /api/install answers 204 or 400. /graphiql is OFF unless ENABLE_GRAPHIQL is set, and the Prometheus endpoint lives on its own port (METRICS_PORT, default 9000) which this compose does not publish, which matters because METRICS_USERNAME and METRICS_PASSWORD are both empty by default and an empty pair means NO authentication on it. Moderation, admin and every account action require a token."
  - "REGISTRATION IS OPEN AFTER THE INSTALL, BY DESIGN, AND EMAIL IS OFF, WHICH IS THE PART TO SAY OUT LOUD. models/tenant/tenant.ts:192-202 gives a fresh tenant local auth ENABLED with allowRegistration TRUE on both the stream and the admin target, and :239-242 leaves email DISABLED. So any reader can create an account and comment the moment you finish the install, which is what a commenting platform is for, but with no mailer configured there is no address confirmation, no password reset and no notification mail: accounts are created against unverified addresses. Two consequences to hand over. First, if the admin password is lost there is NO recovery path until SMTP is configured in Settings, so keep it. Second, decide with the user whether the stream should be pre-moderated on day one, and configure SMTP in the admin before inviting anyone."
  - "allowedOrigins IS WHERE THE STREAM IS EMBEDDED, NOT WHERE CORAL LIVES, AND THAT IS THE ONE FIELD OF THE INSTALL THAT NEEDS THE USER'S ANSWER. app/middleware/csp.ts:139-165 turns a site's allowedOrigins into the frame-ancestors CSP for the comment stream, so it must list the ORIGINS OF THE WEBSITE the comments appear on, for example https://www.theirsite.com. Putting only the redu hostname in there produces a Coral that installs cleanly, serves its admin perfectly, and refuses to render inside their actual page. Ask which domains before you install; more can be added in the admin afterwards."
  - "⚠️ LIVE COMMENT UPDATES USE A WEBSOCKET AND NOBODY HAS CONFIRMED REDU'S PROXY UPGRADES IT. Coral's stream subscribes over /api/graphql/live. If the upgrade does not pass through, the failure is quiet: comments still post and still appear on reload, they simply do not stream in. config.ts:267-274 provides the honest fallback, DISABLE_LIVE_UPDATES=true, which turns the feature off across the whole installation and CANNOT be turned back on from the interface, so do not set it pre-emptively. ON THE FIRST REAL DEPLOY, post a comment from a second browser and watch whether it appears without a reload, then write the answer into this file by hand."
  - "USERNAME AND PASSWORD RULES FOR THE ADMIN YOU CREATE, BOTH ENFORCED SERVER-SIDE AND BOTH EASY TO TRIP. common/lib/helpers/validate.ts:3-5: the username must match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_.]+$ and be 3 to 30 characters, which means NO HYPHEN: a generated name like coral-admin is rejected outright, so use coral_admin or coraladmin. validate.ts:9: the password minimum is 8 characters. Generate it locally and alphanumeric only, both because this library's rule says so and because the install body is JSON, where an unescaped quote or backslash would make the request invalid rather than merely wrong."

# Self-host Coral on redu

Comments on your own site, on your own server: the commenting platform built by Vox Media and used
by The Washington Post and the Financial Times, on one VM with its own MongoDB and Redis beside it
and a public HTTPS URL. Around GBP 35 a month.

## What this deploys

- **Coral** from the official image, pinned to `9.11.8`, on one m1.large VM, port 5000.
- **MongoDB** and **Redis** in the same compose, on volumes on that VM.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS, which is where the comment stream is served from
  and where you embed it into your own pages.

About GBP 0.049/hour. **Above the no-card trial ceiling**, so this one needs a card.

## Read this before you approve the plan

**The database lives on the app VM.** redu has no managed MongoDB, so unlike every other entry in
this library there is no managed database standing behind this deployment. Every comment, every
reader account and every moderation decision sits on the app VM's disk and shares that VM's
lifetime.

That is workable and it is what upstream's own Docker install does. It just means two things are
on you rather than on the platform:

- **Take backups.** `mongodump`, copied off the VM, on a schedule you choose, and one before
  every redeploy.
- **Deleting the deployment deletes the comments.** There is nothing left behind to restore from.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Coral on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The one that would actually break it

**Coral has no accounts until somebody runs the installer, and the installer is one unauthenticated
POST that makes the caller an administrator.** No token, no environment variable, no setting closes
that window. From the moment the hostname answers until somebody claims it, the instance belongs to
whoever gets there first.

So the install is part of the deploy, not a thing you do afterwards over coffee. The script below
does it and then proves the window is shut.

Two smaller ones that follow from it:

- **Install through the public hostname.** Coral records the tenant's domain from the Host header
  of the install request, and looks the tenant up by hostname on every request afterwards. Install
  via localhost and the public URL has no tenant at all.
- **`allowedOrigins` is your website, not Coral's address.** It becomes the `frame-ancestors`
  policy for the stream, so it decides where the comments are allowed to be embedded.

## The compose

Three services, one published port. Upstream ships no production compose, so this is written from
the Dockerfile and the configuration source.

```yaml
services:
  talk:
    image: coralproject/talk:9.11.8
    restart: unless-stopped
    depends_on:
      - mongo
      - redis
    ports:
      - "5000:5000"
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: "production"
      PORT: "5000"
      MONGODB_URI: "mongodb://mongo:[REDACTED:conn-password]/coral"
      REDIS_URI: "redis://redis:[REDACTED:conn-password]"
      SIGNING_SECRET: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      TRUST_PROXY: "1"
      LOGGING_LEVEL: "info"
  mongo:
    image: mongo:8.0.3
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - coral-mongo:/data/db
  redis:
    image: redis:7.2.5
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes"]
    volumes:
      - coral-redis:/data
volumes:
  coral-mongo:
  coral-redis:
```

`CORAL_SIGNING_SECRET` goes in a `.env` beside it, generated locally with
`openssl rand -base64 45`. Note that **neither datastore publishes a port**: they are reached by
service name on the compose network. Upstream's root compose publishes both, which is a
development convenience and not something to copy onto a server.

## Claiming the instance

Run this the moment the deploy reports ready, before you hand the URL to anyone.

It **proves it is talking to Coral before it asserts anything** (a 502 from the proxy while the
container starts is not a pass), it refuses to run if somebody has already installed, and it
finishes by actually signing in with the account it created rather than trusting a status code.
Exits `2` rather than passing when it cannot tell.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Claim a fresh Coral before anyone else can, then prove the window is shut.
#   CORAL_ADMIN_EMAIL=you@example.com CORAL_ADMIN_USERNAME=coral_admin \
#   CORAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD=[REDACTED:value] CORAL_ORG_NAME="Your Org" CORAL_ORG_URL=https://www.example.com \
#   CORAL_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=https://www.example.com \
#     ./claim-coral.sh coral-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = claimed, 1 = NOT safe / already taken, 2 = inconclusive (may still be starting; re-run).
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: claim-coral.sh <host>}"
: "${CORAL_ADMIN_EMAIL:?admin email}"
: "${CORAL_ADMIN_USERNAME:?admin username, 3-30 chars of a-z A-Z 0-9 _ . and NO hyphen}"
: "${CORAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD:«REDACTED:assigned:953a8a9a» password, at least 8 characters}"
: "${CORAL_ORG_NAME:?organisation name}"
: "${CORAL_ORG_URL:?organisation url, e.g. https://www.example.com}"
: "${CORAL_ALLOWED_ORIGINS:?the site origin the comments get embedded on}"

case "$CORAL_ADMIN_USERNAME" in
  *[!A-Za-z0-9_.]*) echo "FAIL: username may only contain a-z A-Z 0-9 _ . (no hyphen)." >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
case "$CORAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD" in
  *[!A-Za-z0-9]*) echo "FAIL: generate the password alphanumeric only; this goes into JSON." >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
for v in "$CORAL_ORG_NAME" "$CORAL_ORG_URL" "$CORAL_ALLOWED_ORIGINS" "$CORAL_ADMIN_EMAIL"; do
  case "$v" in
    *'"'*|*'\'*) echo "FAIL: a quote or backslash in "$v" would corrupt the JSON body." >&2; exit 1 ;;
  esac
done
[ "${#CORAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD}" -ge 8 ] || { echo "FAIL: password must be at least 8 characters." >&2; exit 1; }

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# 1. GATE: is this actually Coral, and is it up? Everything below is vacuous otherwise.
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/ver" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/version")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/version answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
  if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
    echo "  502 is redu's proxy while the container starts. Re-run; NOT a pass." >&2
  fi
  exit 2
fi
grep -q '"version"' "$TMP/ver" || {
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200, but the body is not Coral's version document." >&2
  echo "  Something else is answering on this hostname. Do not read this as safe." >&2
  exit 2
}

# 2. Is the instance still unclaimed? 204 = nobody has installed. 400 = someone has.
#    This route also touches MongoDB and Redis, which /api/health does not.
pre=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/install")
case "$pre" in
  204) ;;
  400) echo "FAIL: this Coral is ALREADY INSTALLED and it was not you." >&2
       echo "  Someone else owns the admin account. Do not leave it running: tear it down" >&2
       echo "  and redeploy, then claim it within the same step." >&2
       exit 1 ;;
  *)   echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/install answered HTTP $pre, expected 204 or 400." >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac

# 3. Claim it. The body goes to curl from a FILE, never in argv, because an argument is
#    visible in ps to every user on the box.
cat > "$TMP/body.json" <<JSON
{
  "tenant": {
    "organization": {
      "name": "$CORAL_ORG_NAME",
      "url": "$CORAL_ORG_URL",
      "contactEmail": "$CORAL_ADMIN_EMAIL"
    },
    "locale": "en-US"
  },
  "site": {
    "name": "$CORAL_ORG_NAME",
    "allowedOrigins": ["$CORAL_ALLOWED_ORIGINS"]
  },
  "user": {
    "username": "$CORAL_ADMIN_USERNAME",
    "password": "[REDACTED:value]",
    "email": "$CORAL_ADMIN_EMAIL"
  }
}
JSON

inst=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/inst" -w '%{http_code}' \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  --data-binary @"$TMP/body.json" "https://$HOST/api/install")
if [ "$inst" != "204" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: POST /api/install answered HTTP $inst, not 204." >&2
  echo "  Response: $(cat "$TMP/inst")" >&2
  echo "  Common causes: a hyphen in the username, a password under 8 characters," >&2
  echo "  a non-URL organisation url, or the per-IP limit of 1 install per 10 seconds." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# 4. NEGATIVE half: the window must now be shut.
post=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/install")
[ "$post" = "400" ] || {
  echo "FAIL: after installing, /api/install still answers HTTP $post." >&2
  echo "  The instance may still be claimable. Do not hand out this URL." >&2
  exit 1
}

# 5. POSITIVE half, and it is what makes step 4 mean anything: YOUR account signs in.
printf '{"email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CORAL_ADMIN_EMAIL" "$CORAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD" > "$TMP/login.json"
login=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/tok" -w '%{http_code}' \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  --data-binary @"$TMP/login.json" "https://$HOST/api/auth/local")
[ "$login" = "200" ] || { echo "FAIL: the admin account does not sign in (HTTP $login)." >&2; exit 1; }
grep -q '"token"' "$TMP/tok" || { echo "FAIL: sign-in returned no token." >&2; exit 1; }

echo "OK: Coral is installed, the install route now refuses, and your admin account signs in."
echo "    Next, in the admin at https://$HOST/admin: configure SMTP (email is OFF by default,"
echo "    so there is no password reset until you do), and decide your moderation defaults."
```

Both are also in `deploy/.env` (secret) locally and nowhere in `redu.md`. **Keep the password** — email is off by default, so there is no password-reset path until you configure SMTP in the admin.

## The install window is shut

I claimed it as part of the deploy, through the public hostname so the tenant's domain is the real one. Verified three ways, not one: `GET /api/install` now answers **400** (was 204), and the account I created **actually signs in** and returns a token. `allowedOrigins` is `https://[infra-host]` — that's the `frame-ancestors` policy, so the stream will embed there and nowhere else until you add more origins in the admin.

## Both open questions in redu.md are now settled

- **AVX: present.** `grep -c avx /proc/cpuinfo` = 4, and mongo:8.0.3 logs "Waiting for connections". MongoDB runs fine on this flavor.
- **Websocket: upgrades.** `/api/graphql/live` returns `101 Switching Protocols` through openresty with the `graphql-ws` subprotocol echoed back, so `DISABLE_LIVE_UPDATES` stays unset. One trap worth knowing: test it with `curl --http1.1`, because over HTTP/2 there is no Upgrade mechanism and Coral answers with a `400 RAW_QUERY_NOT_AUTHORIZED` that reads exactly like a proxy refusing to upgrade. I hit that and it is not a failure.
- **Idle memory:** talk 196 MiB, mongo 101 MiB, redis 7 MiB; 985 MB of 7941 MB VM-wide, 6.1 GB of 77 GB disk. Generous — but there are no comments in the database yet, so it is not grounds for downsizing. WiredTiger grows with the corpus.

## Your data is on this VM

`app-src-mongo-1` writes to a docker volume on the app VM's disk. There is no managed database behind it, so `delete_deployment` destroys every comment and account with nothing to restore from. Backup, run on the VM and copied off it:

```
sudo docker exec app-src-mongo-1 mongodump --archive --db=coral | gzip > coral-$(date +%F).archive.gz
```

Take one before every redeploy and before any image bump — a migration is the one operation with no undo.

## Still worth doing

Registration is open to anyone the moment you share the URL, against unverified email addresses, since there is no mailer. Before you invite readers: configure SMTP in the admin, and decide whether the stream should be pre-moderated. The one thing I could not test from here is end-to-end live updates in a browser — open two windows, post in one, and see whether it appears in the other without a reload. The protocol half passes; that confirms the product half.
